threatModel.summary: Jubarte is an in-process Rust document engine for comparison, tracked edits, inspection, validation, sanitization, legacy DOC import, Markdown conversion, and PDF/PNG rendering. It accepts complete document bytes and returns generated bytes or reports (src/lib.rs:7-35). Hosts include the native CLI, Python/PyO3 library and CLI, browser/Node WASM bindings, Node CLI, and optional Python stdio MCP server (jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:5-15; jubarte-python/pyproject.toml:42-49; jubarte-wasm/src/lib.rs:7-28). Normal processing is local; native rendering additionally reads installed fonts and persists a font index. CLI self-update and privileged installation/publication workflows have separate network and filesystem authority. MCP supplies capability-confined document I/O, whereas CLI paths use the invoking account's ambient authority.
assets: Confidential input document text, revisions, comments, embedded media, metadata, and generated document/PDF/PNG/report contents; MCP explicitly returns document text through designated tools (docs/adoption/mcp.md:69-75).

Integrity and availability of the hosting process and document transformations: untrusted ZIP/XML, legacy DOC, fonts, and images reach native parsing/rendering code; unsafe Rust is forbidden in the engine itself (src/lib.rs; SECURITY.md:35-74).

Filesystem contents reachable through MCP's granted root versus ambient CLI paths; OutputRoot holds an open cap_std directory capability, while publish_paths explicitly grants ambient local access (src/publication.rs:146-165,203-225).

Native font files and persistent font-resolution metadata. Supplemental fonts resolve from JUBARTE_FONT_DIR or platform user-data directories; the index defaults to font-index.tsv beside, rather than inside, the fonts directory (src/convert/font.rs:2637-2652,3098-3107).

Installed executable integrity during self-update. Current compiled release verification keys are empty and the first signed release is unset; updates therefore rely on release SHA-256 checksums and transport/release authority (src/update.rs:25-48,198-210,245-257).

Release signing authority, GitHub release write authority, and separate crates.io/npm/PyPI publication credentials (.github/workflows/release.yml:230-235,261-307,356-369; scripts/release.sh:370-380,875-899).
trustBoundaries: Document supplier to engine: attacker-controlled DOCX bytes cross archive admission, OPC loading, XML validation, comparison/editing, and rendering. Default admission allows 64 MiB compressed, 10,000 entries, 64 MiB per part, 256 MiB inflated, and XML depth 256; comparison permits 512 MiB compressed/per part and 2 GiB inflated (src/admission.rs:63-100). Structural ZIP checks compare central/local records and reject recorded defects; actual decompression is bounded independently of declared sizes (src/admission.rs:439-470; src/opc/archive.rs:34-51; src/opc/mod.rs:275-324).

Caller-controlled input limits to binding configuration: Python and WASM parse overrides through InputLimitOverrides and apply them over comparison settings. Unknown keys are rejected; applications own any decision to raise or lower these limits (src/admission.rs:103-138; jubarte-python/src/lib.rs:65-79; jubarte-wasm/src/lib.rs:63-85).

Raw XML library caller to DOM: parse_xdocument is intentionally permissive and does not enforce input policy; try_parse_xdocument_with_limits validates before constructing a DOM (src/xmllinq/parse.rs:90-135). Package admission must not be inferred for arbitrary direct XML API use.

MCP client/model to filesystem tools: --root defaults to startup cwd and is resolved once; path arguments receive Python containment diagnostics, but actual document reads/publication use native OutputRoot (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:67-108,373-381). OutputRoot is the enforcement owner, not MCP annotations. Read-only/destructive hints are tool metadata, and client approval remains host-owned (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:54-55; docs/adoption/mcp.md:39-41).

MCP publication: edits derive clean.docx, redline.docx, patch.diff and report.json below caller-selected out_dir; optional render products share that directory. Native publication validates names and stages every output before committing, rejects unsafe paths, and uses overwrite=false unless granted. Commit atomicity is per file, not across the set; errors identify already committed files (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:152-217; src/publication.rs:83-143,168-199).

Native CLI to filesystem: document input paths are read with std::fs::read; authorized output paths are handed to ambient publication. There is no MCP-style root capability for the entire CLI (src/bin/jubarte.rs:261-273,2740-2756; src/publication.rs:203-225). Python Document.read and Node CLI similarly read explicitly supplied paths; Node writes use fs.writeFileSync (jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/document.py:142-145; jubarte-wasm/cli/bin/jubarte-redlines.mjs:52-73,106-111).

Markdown-controlled image references to local resources: the native CLI resolves --resource-path or the Markdown input's resource directory, percent-decodes targets, refuses URL schemes and escapes, then reads through a held OutputRoot capability (src/bin/jubarte.rs:2811-2870,3365-3375). Library DocxOptions instead accepts a caller-provided ImageLoader callback and defaults to no loader; callback authority belongs to the embedding application (src/markdown/mod.rs:159-170).

Native render request to ambient font state: requested families select installed/supplemental font searches and FONT_INDEX lookups. These reads and index writes use ambient fs operations, independent of MCP document-root confinement (src/convert/font.rs:2258-2315,2637-2652,3154-3188,3213-3227). Windows system font locations derive from WINDIR, then SystemRoot, then C:\Windows, plus LOCALAPPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\Fonts (src/convert/font.rs:2855-2862).

Edit requester to document mutation: optional source_sha256 binds a schema-1 plan to the exact source snapshot and mismatches produce STALE_SOURCE. This is a consistency guard, not authentication or approval (src/edit.rs:2074-2089; SECURITY.md:76-85).

Maintainer debug mode to malformed packages: debug intentionally uses open_archive_unchecked so rejected archives can be inspected, unlike ordinary package loading; this materially different parser path must retain its own resource assessment (src/debug.rs:213; src/opc/archive.rs:15-20,34-51).

Operator to self-update: only the explicit self-update command invokes update::run. It selects jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines releases, platform asset and archive binary path, SHA256SUMS.txt, optional signature verification, and an extracted-regular-file hook before delegated replacement (src/bin/jubarte.rs:4062-4073; src/update.rs:25-48,186-210,234-257,299-321).

Maintainer/tag authority to distribution: v* tags trigger read-only build jobs and a separate contents:write release job. Optional signing receives ZIPSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY only in its step, decodes it beneath RUNNER_TEMP, and removes temporary keys on exit; GitHub publication receives GITHUB_TOKEN separately (.github/workflows/release.yml:15-21,230-307,356-369). Local release.sh independently confirms the target version unless --yes, pushes release state, and publishes using operator registry identities (scripts/release.sh:875-899).
attackerCapabilities: A document author can supply malformed DOCX/ZIP/XML, legacy DOC, embedded fonts/images, document metadata, and Markdown image destinations to an application that processes such input. The author does not thereby control environment variables, MCP root, process identity, registry credentials, or release keys.

An MCP client can invoke exposed read and write tools using paths under the granted root, select output directories and overwrite=true, and receive intentionally exposed document contents. No per-user or per-tenant separation is established inside that root; host process launch and tool approval define caller authority.

A malicious document can cause parsing/rendering work and family lookups, but filesystem image reads in the native Markdown loader remain separately confined to its resource root. Embedding applications may grant more authority through their own ImageLoader.

A party controlling a release asset or privileged publication account would affect a different supply-chain boundary from an ordinary document supplier. Current checksum-only updating does not provide an independent compiled signing-key identity.
An attacker who already controls the invoking account's CLI paths or environment has that account's authority; ordinary authorized local I/O is not itself a privilege escalation.

A distinct local principal with write access to a shared output/plan directory may substitute directory entries while the victim CLI runs, without already being able to modify victim-owned referents elsewhere. Shared-directory use is conditional, not a default deployment assumption.
securityObjectives: Reject unsafe or ambiguous package identities and structurally inconsistent ZIP content before ordinary processing, and bound actual inflated bytes rather than trusting archive metadata (src/admission.rs:439-470; src/opc/mod.rs:275-324).

Enforce active XML tag, attribute, namespace, and depth policies before checked DOM construction. Default XML caps include 1,024 attributes, 1,024-byte qualified attribute names, 64 MiB attribute values, and 128 MiB start tags (src/xmllinq/parse.rs:49-57,119-135).

Keep MCP document reads and output publication inside its granted directory capability even when symlinks change, and preserve existing destinations unless overwrite is authorized (src/publication.rs:146-199; jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/mcp_server.py:91-108).
Keep native Markdown image loading inside the explicitly selected resource root and never fetch URL destinations through that loader (src/bin/jubarte.rs:2811-2870).

Preserve edit snapshot consistency where hashes are supplied and report refusals before publication; distinguish transformation refusal from later filesystem commit failures (src/edit.rs:2074-2089; src/publication.rs:83-143).

Limit self-update to an explicit operator action and platform-selected executable; verify configured checksums/signatures and reject extracted nonregular binaries before replacement (src/update.rs:186-257,299-321).
Keep release signing, GitHub publication, and registry publication authority separate from untrusted document processing.
assumptions: No user deployment context, knowledge base, supplied threat model, or scoped inventory was provided. Source mapping does not establish a public service, network exposure, tenancy, actual installed versions, host mounts, live credentials, registry permissions, or external branch-protection settings.

Applicable root SECURITY.md covers the engine, CLI and Python/WASM bindings. Its requirement for host process memory/CPU limits remains a caller obligation; input limits do not establish complete denial-of-service protection (SECURITY.md:9-11,71-74).

The model distinguishes default and comparison budgets. WASM source explicitly warns that its default comparison budget can exceed a 32-bit WASM heap and instructs browser hosts to lower it (jubarte-wasm/src/lib.rs:80-85).

Documentation says the byte-oriented toolkit uses no temporary files (src/lib.rs:7-11), while native rendering's font index writes a sibling temporary file before rename (src/convert/font.rs:3213-3227). This is a documentation qualification/disagreement about rendering side effects, not a demonstrated vulnerability. README.md:907-920 separately documents persistent font-index configuration and disabling it.

MCP documentation promises confinement of path arguments and output products (docs/adoption/mcp.md:61-70). That capability does not sandbox the entire native renderer: installed-font reads and font-index writes retain ambient process access (src/convert/font.rs:2637-2652,3154-3188,3213-3227). Actual fonts/index environment and host permissions are unknown.

Current compiled signing configuration is checksum-only (src/update.rs:44-48), consistent with the staged-signing description in docs/SELF_UPDATE.md:67-79. Whether CI has an optional signing secret is unknown; a configured CI secret alone would not add trusted keys to existing binaries.

Direct permissive XML parsing and maintainer debug archive opening are deliberate exceptions; generic claims that every exposed API enforces full admission must retain these exceptions (src/xmllinq/parse.rs:90-135; src/opc/archive.rs:15-20).

External dependency extraction/replacement internals, generated WASM equivalence, all publication call sites, browser embedding policy, and exhaustive parser/callback reachability were not fully reviewed. Architecture mapping is not completed security-audit coverage.

Repository security policy names rdocx-opc 0.2 (SECURITY.md:89-98), while the effective dependency is oxml-opc 0.14.2 with default features disabled (Cargo.toml:102-117; src/opc/mod.rs:29-51,222-251). This stale policy statement is a documentation/configuration discrepancy, not by itself a vulnerability.

findings.title: Converting a Markdown drawing with cyclic dependencies aborts the process
findings.summary: An attacker who supplies Markdown to `markdown_to_docx` can encode a `drawing:` payload whose internal part relationship points back to itself. Materialization recursively follows the index without a visiting set or depth bound, exhausting the stack and terminating the conversion host.

severity.rationale: A small attacker-controlled input reliably reaches an unbounded recursive parser operation. The supported impact is availability loss of the conversion process; a shared long-lived host must accept untrusted Markdown for cross-user disruption.
severity.changeConditions: A one-shot isolated CLI worker limits the impact; a shared long-lived conversion service increases it. No remote deployment is assumed.

confidence.rationale: The public input, base64/JSON decoding, package materialization and unconditional recursive edge are directly source-established; no runtime payload was executed.

codeEvidence.label: Public Markdown conversion input
codeEvidence.explanation: A library caller supplies the Markdown string, so input from a lower-trust document producer can reach this boundary without filesystem privileges.

codeEvidence.label: Drawing destinations deserialize without graph validation
codeEvidence.explanation: The destination controls deserialized Drawing.rels and Drawing.deps, including numeric part indexes. JSON nesting protection cannot detect a cycle expressed by indexes.

codeEvidence.label: Accepted drawing is stored for package output
codeEvidence.explanation: Successfully decoded input becomes a Content::Drawing item; it is not restricted to payloads previously generated by the product.

codeEvidence.label: Internal index starts recursive materialization
codeEvidence.explanation: A top-level relationship with part=0 and no external URL reaches the first attacker-controlled dependency.

codeEvidence.label: Dependency index is recursively followed without a cycle guard
codeEvidence.explanation: A dependency whose relationship also has part=0 repeatedly invokes the same index. The used set tracks output names and never checks active dependency indexes. No bytes are written or duplicate-part reuse checked until recursion returns.

rootCause.summary: `Drawing` deserialization accepts internal relationship indexes from a Markdown destination. `Writer::picture` stores the graph and `PartRelate::drawing` calls `materialize`. Each internal edge invokes `dep_part`, which reserves a name and follows further indexes before storing the part. It lacks an active-index set, memoization or recursion budget, so a self-edge never reaches the later byte-deduplication check.

findings.remediation: Validate decoded dependency graphs and materialize with a visiting/complete state per dependency index. Reject cycles with a recoverable MarkdownError and enforce depth, part-count and aggregate-byte budgets before traversal.

counterEvidence: MAX_DEPS, MAX_DEP_RELS and MAX_DEP_BYTES bound DOCX-to-Markdown capture, not Drawing decode or materialization.
The output-name used set and later byte deduplication do not detect active graph cycles.
The repository recommends process limits; those constrain the failure to a process but do not turn stack exhaustion into a recoverable conversion error.
limitations: Static validation only; no shared service deployment or exploit runtime was assumed.
validation.summary: Confirmed a graph with one dependency and a self-referencing part index is accepted by decode and recursively revisited without a terminating condition. Public conversion assembles the package before any post-conversion revision processing. No test or triggering input was run.

dataflow.summary: Markdown string -> Writer::picture -> drawing::decode -> Content::Drawing -> package assembly -> PartRelate::drawing -> materialize -> dep_part -> same dep_part index indefinitely.

impact.why: Denial of service to the conversion process.

likelihood.why: A single small graph cycle deterministically reaches the recursive edge without a depth or cycle guard.

reachability.summary: Reachable through the public Markdown-to-DOCX library/parser boundary. The attacker needs control of converted Markdown, not server configuration or output paths.
preconditions: A host converts Markdown supplied by an attacker.

attackPath.summary: Supply a Markdown image with a base64 JSON drawing envelope that points to dependency 0, whose own relationship also points to 0, then request Markdown-to-DOCX conversion.

remediationTests: Reject a one-node self-cycle and a two-node cycle without aborting the process.
Preserve shared acyclic dependencies and reject over-budget dependency graphs.

findings.title: Rendering a DOCX with an oversized HTML table span exhausts memory
findings.summary: An attacker-supplied DOCX can embed a small HTML altChunk with a huge `colspan`. The renderer trusts that number as a table column count and appends a grid entry for every column before layout, allowing a tiny admitted package to allocate gigabytes and terminate the conversion process.

severity.rationale: Small untrusted document input deterministically drives a large CPU and memory expansion in standard rendering. The demonstrated impact is process availability; shared-service exposure is conditional.
severity.changeConditions: A memory-limited isolated worker reduces the blast radius. A long-lived shared host accepting untrusted DOCX increases the availability impact.

confidence.rationale: The package load, HTML parsing, attacker-controlled usize and unbounded output loop are directly visible in source; no runtime exploit was executed.

codeEvidence.label: Admitted document loads an internal HTML chunk
codeEvidence.explanation: DOCX relationship and part bytes controlled by the document producer are imported before the renderer constructs its DOM. Network or filesystem relationships are not needed.

codeEvidence.label: HTML body is converted before return
codeEvidence.explanation: The chunk is decoded into HTML and fully converted to a WML string with no expansion budget passed into html_to_wml.

codeEvidence.label: HTML colspan becomes an unbounded usize
codeEvidence.explanation: A numeric colspan such as one billion remains valid on supported 32- and 64-bit hosts; only a lower bound is applied.

codeEvidence.label: Spans determine expanded column count
codeEvidence.explanation: A one-cell row transfers its attacker-controlled span directly to cols. The width calculation does not cap the number of columns.

codeEvidence.label: One string append per attacker-selected column
codeEvidence.explanation: The output String expands linearly with the numeric value, rather than the input length. The loop has no column, iteration or byte budget.

rootCause.summary: The DOCX renderer expands local altChunk HTML after package admission. `Builder::start` converts the HTML cell's `colspan` to `usize` and applies only a minimum of one. `end_table` sums these spans, then emits one `w:gridCol` per unit into a growing String. The decoded input budgets limit the small source chunk but do not constrain this generated output.

findings.remediation: Bound individual spans, total table columns and total generated WML bytes before building table grids. Use checked arithmetic and return a recoverable input-limit error for excessive expansion; apply the same budget throughout altChunk import.

counterEvidence: Package admission bounds archive and inflated part bytes, but the HTML remains small and the expansion occurs afterward.
External relationship resolution is not required; an ordinary internal HTML part is sufficient.
Process memory/CPU limits are documented caller controls and do not prevent the small-input amplification inside a worker.
limitations: No runtime triggering document was generated or executed; remote or shared deployment was not asserted.
validation.summary: Confirmed normal PDF/PNG layout imports internal HTML parts, parses a single large but valid colspan and loops exactly that many times before DOM creation. A one-cell HTML table requires no large archive, excessive XML depth or integer overflow.

dataflow.summary: DOCX main part -> altChunk relationship -> internal HTML bytes -> html_to_wml -> Builder::start colspan -> Cell.span -> end_table cols -> repeated String growth.

impact.why: Availability loss of the conversion process.

likelihood.why: The numeric column count directly controls an unconditional expansion loop.

reachability.summary: The public rendering pipeline accepts untrusted DOCX packages and expands the HTML chunk after admission. The attacker only needs control of document content.
reachability.entrypoint: Public PDF/PNG conversion and shared layout pipeline
reachability.outcome: CPU/memory exhaustion and possible process termination.

attackPath.summary: Submit a DOCX whose body references an internal HTML altChunk containing a table cell with an extremely large positive colspan, then request PDF/PNG conversion or another layout-dependent operation.

remediationTests: Reject an oversized colspan in a small admitted DOCX without allocating proportional output.
Cover aggregate spans across multiple cells and arithmetic overflow while preserving normal merged tables.

findings.title: Python and Node plan recording can overwrite files through predictable staging symlinks
findings.summary: A different local user who can create entries in the selected plan directory can precreate the internal PID-based partial pathname as a symlink. Python and Node open that pathname with truncation, corrupting a victim-writable file outside the selected plan before renaming the symlink into place.

severity.rationale: Source establishes unauthorized file corruption, but exploitation is constrained to a shared/attacker-writable plan directory, a predictable process ID, and an OS permitting this symlink write. No remote path or code execution is established.
severity.changeConditions: Private trusted plan directories prevent this attack. Routine processing in hostile shared directories or a more privileged CLI account increases impact and likelihood.

confidence.rationale: Both bindings explicitly build predictable partial names and use symlink-following default truncating writes. The native writer's independent control does not protect these call sites.

codeEvidence.label: Python plan staging follows existing symlinks
codeEvidence.code:
target = Path(os.path.realpath(plan))
        partial = target.with_name(f".{target.name}.{os.getpid()}.partial")
        try:
            partial.write_bytes(recorded["json"].encode("utf-8"))
            os.replace(partial, target)
codeEvidence.explanation: The internally derived PID-based pathname is opened with truncating Path.write_bytes, allowing an attacker-created symlink to select the written file.

codeEvidence.label: Node plan staging follows existing symlinks
codeEvidence.explanation: The same predictable staging path is opened with default fs.writeFileSync flags before rename; neither exclusive creation nor symlink refusal occurs.

codeEvidence.label: Native plan writer uses secure publication
codeEvidence.explanation: The native implementation delegates the equivalent write to staged publication; the language CLI writers instead implement their own unsafe staging.

rootCause.summary: After plan validation, `_record` and `recordPlan` resolve the selected plan, append a process ID to derive a partial filename, and write through that filename. Default write modes follow an existing symbolic link and truncate its referent before the subsequent atomic rename. Resolving the user-selected plan does not validate the separately created staging name.

findings.remediation: Create staging files exclusively inside a private unpredictable directory, keep the descriptor open while writing and atomically publish the verified bytes. Reuse native publication for Python; provide equivalent secure publication for Node rather than reopening predictable partial paths.

counterEvidence: The plan and preview must succeed, but they validate edits rather than staging-file identity.
Intentional handling of an explicit user-selected plan symlink does not authorize an attacker-created internal temporary symlink.
Native write_plan uses publication::publish_paths and tests/cli_plan_record.rs:2280-2288 protects the same scenario; both language writers bypass it.
Filesystem protected-symlink settings and private directories can block this conditional local attack.
limitations: No runtime race, filesystem mutation or application execution was performed.
No arbitrary code execution or MCP root escape is established.
validation.summary: Confirmed entry through edit/add recording with --plan and operation flags. A precreated internal partial symlink redirects the write before rename. The attacker needs directory-entry rights, not write access to the victim-owned referent.

dataflow.summary: Operator plan path -> derived predictable partial path -> attacker-created symlink -> default truncating write -> victim-owned referent; rename then moves the link.

impact.why: Integrity loss outside the authorized plan path; content is constrained to generated plan JSON.

likelihood.why: Requires conditional local shared-directory use and symlink staging.

reachability.summary: Local shared-directory attack against Python/Node edit/add plan recording. An ordinary document author without directory access cannot trigger it.
reachability.outcome: Unauthorized corruption of a victim-writable file with generated plan JSON.
preconditions: The victim selects a plan directory writable by the attacker.
The attacker predicts or observes the victim PID and the OS permits following the symlink.

attackPath.summary: While a victim records a plan in a writable shared directory, precreate .<plan-name>.<victim-pid>.partial pointing to a file the victim can write. The CLI writes plan JSON through the link.

remediationTests: Precreate the old predictable partial pathname as a symlink and verify its referent remains unchanged in Python and Node.
Verify failed staging preserves the existing plan and cleans only operation-owned temporary entries.

originalCandidate.originalEvidence: Candidate found in Node CLI plan recording: jubarte-wasm/cli/bin/jubarte-redlines.mjs:420-423 uses predictable .${basename}.${process.pid}.partial and fs.writeFileSync(partial, recorded.json) without exclusive/no-follow flags, then rename. A distinct local user with write access to the plan directory can preplace this staging name as a symlink to a file writable by the invoking victim, causing truncation/overwrite outside the chosen plan path. Investigating sibling writers and exact impact/counterevidence before final JSON.
originalCandidate.additionalEvidence: Confirmed same predictable staging in Python CLI independently: jubarte-python/python/jubarte_redlines/__main__.py:407-411 (.{target.name}.{os.getpid()}.partial, partial.write_bytes, os.replace). Native Rust fixed via publication staging in src/edit/record.rs; tests/cli_plan_record.rs:2280-2288 protects predictable partial symlinks. Both bindings bypass native writer. MCP _OutputRoot confinement/no-clobber appears effective for client-only attackers via cap-std held directory, exclusive scratch, atomic hard-link commit.

findings.title: Python and Node CLI output races bypass no-overwrite checks
findings.summary: A different local directory writer can insert an output symlink after Python or Node checks that a destination is absent. The final default write follows the link and truncates a file writable by the victim, even when --force was not supplied.

severity.rationale: The source establishes file corruption across distinct local principals, but requires a concurrently writable selected output directory and a successful substitution race. Document content alone cannot choose a host path, and private directories prevent this attack.
severity.changeConditions: Shared directories and slow conversion/diff work increase the race opportunity. No remote exploitation or execution gain is established.

confidence.rationale: Both CLI implementations separate existence checks from default truncating writes; representative diff entrypoints and common writer callers were traced.

codeEvidence.label: Python checks existence before processing
codeEvidence.explanation: This checks the name before rendering; it does not bind the final write to the observed absence.

codeEvidence.label: Python diff separates preflight and publication
codeEvidence.code:
output = args.output
    # An existing output is refused before any work.
    if output is not None:
        _ensure_writable(output, args.force)
    old = _read_side(args.old, args.old_format)
    new = _read_side(args.new, args.new_format)
codeEvidence.explanation: The operator output is checked before reading both inputs and computing the diff; another directory writer can insert a link during that interval.

codeEvidence.label: Python final write truncates and follows symlinks
codeEvidence.explanation: The final helper receives no force/no-clobber policy and uses Path.write_bytes, so the earlier absence check is not enforced atomically.

codeEvidence.label: Node checks existence before processing
codeEvidence.explanation: existsSync supplies an early diagnostic only and cannot prevent a subsequent directory-entry substitution.

codeEvidence.label: Node diff performs work after checking output
codeEvidence.explanation: The check precedes input reads and computation, while final publication at line 214 invokes the unguarded writer.

codeEvidence.label: Node final write follows the substituted output
codeEvidence.explanation: fs.writeFileSync defaults to a truncating symlink-following open and does not preserve the no-overwrite flag.

codeEvidence.label: Native publication enforces no overwrite during commit
codeEvidence.code:
// hard_link is an atomic no-clobber installation, including when a
            // hostile writer creates the target after the initial check.
            Phase::Commit => staged
                .scratch
                .as_ref()
                .expect("open staging directory")
                .hard_link("bytes", &staged.parent, &staged.target),
codeEvidence.explanation: The existing native publisher uses atomic hard-link installation, demonstrating the control missing in the language writers.

rootCause.summary: `_ensure_writable`/`ensureWritable` enforce --force using an existence check, but `_write`/`write` receive only a path and bytes. They open the path again with default truncation after processing. A symlink inserted between these operations changes the file receiving the write, without an atomic no-clobber or held-parent publication control.

findings.remediation: Carry overwrite policy to the final publisher and enforce it atomically using securely staged bytes and no-clobber installation. Hold the authorized parent directory where supported; never rely on a repeated exists check. Apply the same publisher to every output and report writer.

counterEvidence: An existing link to an existing file is refused at preflight without --force; the attack inserts it afterward.
The operator must choose an attacker-writable directory; document bytes alone do not grant filesystem path authority.
Native publication and MCP use atomic no-clobber installation and are not affected by this common language-CLI writer.
No claim that a preexisting explicit operator-authorized link with --force is itself an exploit.
limitations: Static trace only; no filesystem race or application code executed.
validation.summary: Confirmed diff routes check the output before reading inputs and computing results, then call the unguarded common writer. The affected writer also serves comparison, conversion, PNG/report/font-report products, revision results, edit/visual-diff bundles, field-update reports and repair outputs.

dataflow.summary: Operator output path -> exists check -> document computation -> attacker substitutes output entry -> Path.write_bytes/fs.writeFileSync -> victim-writable referent.

impact.why: Unauthorized file corruption with generated output bytes.

likelihood.why: Requires conditional shared-directory use and winning a local substitution race.

reachability.summary: A distinct local directory writer can reach common Python/Node output writers without controlling the victim account. The native and MCP publishers enforce a separate boundary.
reachability.entrypoint: Python/Node CLI diff and shared output publication
reachability.outcome: Existing file outside the selected output is overwritten without --force.
preconditions: Attacker can create/replace entries in the selected output directory during the command.
The victim can write the targeted referent and OS symlink controls permit the write.

attackPath.summary: Watch a victim CLI diff/conversion in a writable shared directory; after the absent-output preflight, insert a link at the output name targeting a victim-writable private file. Publication follows that link.

remediationTests: Insert a destination between preflight and publication and verify no-force refuses it without changing its referent.
Cover all side products and verify --force replaces only the selected directory entry rather than following a substituted link.

findings.title: Rendering DOCX table spans can allocate gigabytes from a small document
findings.summary: An untrusted DOCX can set a huge gridSpan, gridBefore or gridAfter. Layout treats those values as actual column counts and sizes column and merge vectors directly from them, causing allocation failure or worker memory exhaustion despite archive/XML admission.

severity.rationale: A small document deterministically controls large allocations during ordinary rendering. Impact is process denial of service; a shared service must accept attacker documents for cross-user disruption.
severity.changeConditions: OS process limits and per-document worker isolation contain the failure. No network service deployment is assumed.

confidence.rationale: Public layout admission, raw numeric parsing, RawCell propagation and span-sized allocations were independently traced in current source.

codeEvidence.label: Unbounded cell gridSpan
codeEvidence.explanation: An attacker-controlled gridSpan is parsed as usize and receives only a minimum bound.

codeEvidence.label: Unbounded row gridBefore/gridAfter
codeEvidence.explanation: Both row skip variants enter the same RawCell occupancy calculation, so fixing cell gridSpan alone is insufficient.

codeEvidence.label: Span-controlled column allocations
codeEvidence.explanation: Summed RawCell spans determine vec and resize lengths independently of input byte count.

codeEvidence.label: Merge bookkeeping also expands to col plus span
codeEvidence.explanation: The later merge state has another span-sized vector, so all geometry-derived allocations need a shared column budget.

rootCause.summary: `cell_span` and `row_grid_skip` accept arbitrary positive usize values and pass them into table geometry. `table_block` sums RawCell.colspan to occupancy and directly allocates/resizes f32 columns to that count. `resolve_table_merges` also resizes state to col+span. No semantic column limit or checked aggregate bound precedes these allocations.

findings.remediation: Validate every cell span and row skip against a shared practical table-column budget before any allocation. Use checked sums and col+span calculations, cap merge-state size and return a typed input refusal for excessive geometry.

counterEvidence: Package admission bounds ZIP/XML bytes, entries and depth but does not enforce these numeric geometry limits.
Width clamping acts on a constructed widths vector and does not bound column count.
The separate HTML table-span remediation does not cover raw OOXML cell/row spans.
Caller process limits constrain the blast radius, not the document's ability to terminate a worker.
limitations: Static analysis only; no allocation-triggering document was run.
validation.summary: Confirmed a one-cell table with gridSpan one billion requests about four billion bytes for an initial f32 vector alone. Row gridBefore/gridAfter reach the same occupancy mechanism through grid_skip_cell. This requires neither altChunk nor a large inflated XML part.

dataflow.summary: DOCX XML -> cell_span / row_grid_skip -> RawCell.colspan -> occupancy sum -> vec!/resize columns -> merge-state resize.

likelihood.why: Numeric spans reach unconditional allocation lengths without a semantic maximum.

reachability.summary: Reachable through standard public layout after admission; attacker controls only document bytes.
reachability.outcome: Huge layout allocations, memory exhaustion or process termination.

attackPath.summary: Provide a DOCX with a small table whose gridSpan or row grid skip requests an excessive number of columns, then request PDF/PNG rendering or layout facts.

remediationTests: Reject huge gridSpan, gridBefore and gridAfter in otherwise small admitted DOCX files.
Cover aggregate span overflow and normal merged cells without large allocation.

originalCandidate.originalEvidence: DOCX w:gridSpan and w:gridBefore/After parse to unbounded usize at convert/mod.rs:14211-14215 / 14339-14346, become RawCell.colspan, summed as occupancy at 13602-13604 then vec![each; occupancy] / cols.resize at 13606-13615; a tiny table with gridSpan=1000000000 requests ~4GB+ vectors. Independent from HTML altChunk parser but same resource-amplification family.

findings.title: A large DOCX numbering level forces billions of lookups or counter allocations
findings.summary: DOCX paragraphs and numbering definitions accept any u32 level. An undefined large level makes the renderer scan every lower integer; defining that level instead makes it initialize every lower counter. A tiny list can monopolize or exhaust the conversion worker.

severity.rationale: Small attacker-controlled document metadata drives an unbounded numeric-range traversal or memory growth in ordinary layout. The established impact is process denial of service.
severity.changeConditions: Process limits and per-document isolation reduce the blast radius; shared long-lived processing increases impact.

confidence.rationale: Unrestricted paragraph/definition parsing and both numeric-range loops were independently verified in current source; no runtime reproduction was needed to establish the dataflow.

codeEvidence.label: Paragraph numbering accepts any u32
codeEvidence.explanation: The paragraph supplies an unrestricted ilvl through normal XML attributes.

codeEvidence.label: Abstract levels accept arbitrary indexes
codeEvidence.explanation: An attacker may define the high level as well as request it, reaching the counter-allocation variant.

codeEvidence.label: Undefined level lookup scans the numeric range
codeEvidence.explanation: Finding a defined parent probes every integer below the requested level instead of iterating actual defined keys.

codeEvidence.label: Defined high level initializes all lower counters
codeEvidence.explanation: A defined large level avoids lookup but inserts a HashMap counter for each lower integer.

codeEvidence.label: Paragraph rendering invokes revised numbering
codeEvidence.explanation: Normal paragraph list rendering reaches numbering with the parsed num_id and ilvl.

rootCause.summary: `num_pr` reads an arbitrary u32 ilvl, and `load_numbering` can store a definition at the same high index. `resolve_ilvl` scans 0..ilvl in reverse when the requested definition is absent. When present, `next_marker` loops 0..resolved and inserts counters even for undefined lower levels. Neither algorithm bounds its work to actual defined levels or a supported semantic range.

findings.remediation: Enforce the supported Word numbering-level range at paragraph, style, abstract and override parsing boundaries. Independently replace numeric-range parent lookup and counter initialization with bounded traversal of actual defined levels.

counterEvidence: Style inheritance has a depth cap but does not bound the resulting ilvl.
Undefined levels eventually find a parent; the numeric-range search still performs the attacker-selected work.
Archive/XML byte and depth caps accept the small numeric attributes.
No network, oversized archive or raised input limits are required.
limitations: No triggering input or application execution was performed.
validation.summary: Confirmed a paragraph level 4,000,000,000 with only level zero defined causes about four billion parent-level probes. Defining the high level moves the failure to lower-counter initialization; fixing only the fallback search leaves that independently reachable operation.

dataflow.summary: Paragraph ilvl / numbering lvl attribute -> num_pr/load_numbering -> list_marker -> resolve_ilvl or next_marker -> numeric-range scan/HashMap growth.

likelihood.why: Both large-level branches retain unconditional attacker-sized loops.

reachability.summary: Attacker-controlled DOCX bytes reach the ordinary public layout parser after admission.
reachability.outcome: Worker CPU exhaustion, excessive counter memory or termination.

attackPath.summary: Supply a numbered paragraph requesting an enormous u32 ilvl and a matching numbering instance; choose an undefined level for CPU exhaustion or define it to trigger counter growth.

remediationTests: Reject excessive paragraph, style, abstract and override level indexes before iteration.
Verify both undefined-high and defined-high level inputs fail promptly while ordinary inherited numbering remains correct.

originalCandidate.originalEvidence: numbering ilvl parsed unrestricted u32 at convert/mod.rs:12711-12714 and w:lvl ilvl 6619-6621. Numbering.resolve_ilvl scans (0..ilvl).rev() 5529-5532; defined high ilvl skips scan but next_marker inserts counters for every level 5613-5633. Tiny list can force billions of iterations/entries. Checking surrounding paths.

findings.title: A DOCX numbering start can allocate a multi-gigabyte Chicago label
findings.summary: An untrusted DOCX can select Chicago numbering with a large u32 start or start override. The shared formatter repeats a marker about start/4 times without a label-size budget, allowing one ordinary level-zero item to request gigabytes during rendering or agent-view reading.

severity.rationale: Tiny admitted numeric metadata deterministically controls a multi-gigabyte allocation in a shared formatter. The impact is conversion/reader process denial of service.
severity.changeConditions: Per-document process isolation limits the failure; shared host processing raises the availability impact.

confidence.rationale: Start parsing, counter initialization, dispatch, repeat allocation and the shared agent-view call were independently traced in current source.

codeEvidence.label: Unrestricted numbering start
codeEvidence.explanation: The document supplies a u32 start with no generated-label length bound.

codeEvidence.label: Numbering instance start overrides
codeEvidence.explanation: Instance overrides and nested level starts reach the same counter and must share the output bound.

codeEvidence.label: Start initializes the active counter
codeEvidence.code:
let start = self
            .starts
            .get(&(num_id.to_string(), resolved))
            .copied()
            .unwrap_or(lvl.start)
            .max(1);
        let cur = *self
            .counters
            .entry((num_id.to_string(), resolved))
            .or_insert(start);
        self.counters
            .insert((num_id.to_string(), resolved), cur.saturating_add(1));
        self.render(&abs, num_id, resolved, &lvl, cur)
    }
codeEvidence.explanation: The original large value is passed to render before the saturating increment can constrain any subsequent use.

codeEvidence.label: Numbering text formats its counter
codeEvidence.explanation: Token replacement calls format_num with the attacker-selected counter value.

codeEvidence.label: Chicago dispatch
codeEvidence.code:
fn format_num(fmt: NumFmt, n: u32) -> String {
    match fmt {
        NumFmt::Decimal => n.to_string(),
        NumFmt::DecimalZero => format!("{n:02}"),
        NumFmt::CardinalText => cardinal_label(n),
        NumFmt::Ordinal => ordinal_label(n),
        NumFmt::OrdinalText => ordinal_text_label(n),
        NumFmt::Hex => format!("{n:X}"),
        NumFmt::Chicago => chicago_label(n),
        NumFmt::IdeographDigital => ideograph_digital_label(n),
codeEvidence.explanation: The chosen format reaches chicago_label directly.

codeEvidence.label: Unbounded symbol repetition
codeEvidence.explanation: repeat allocates proportional to the numeric counter magnitude rather than the input size.

codeEvidence.label: DOCX agent view shares the formatter
codeEvidence.explanation: Document reading also invokes the same list-number formatter, so a rendering-only fix would miss this caller.

rootCause.summary: `parse_num_level` and instance overrides retain unrestricted u32 starts. `next_marker` initializes the active counter from this value and `render` passes it to `format_num`. Chicago formatting computes an index from n-1 and calls String::repeat(index/4+1), without checking output bytes. `list_number` exposes the same formatter to the agent view.

findings.remediation: Enforce an explicit maximum generated numbering-label byte count in the shared formatter, with checked multiplication before repetition and a recoverable refusal or bounded fallback. Apply it to starts, overrides and all read/render callers.

counterEvidence: Saturating counter increments prevent arithmetic wrap but do not cap marker size.
The attack works at normal level zero, so enforcing the supported level range does not fix it.
Input byte/depth/attribute limits do not cap the magnitude of the small numeric start.
An agent-view counter uses the shared formatter and likewise needs the output-length bound.
limitations: No large string was allocated during review; validation is static.
validation.summary: Confirmed start 4,294,967,295 at normal ilvl=0 selects the three-byte double-dagger marker repeated 1,073,741,824 times: 3,221,225,472 requested output bytes. This is independent of excessive numbering levels.

dataflow.summary: DOCX start/startOverride -> numbering counter -> token replacement / agent-view list_number -> format_num Chicago -> chicago_label -> String::repeat.

likelihood.why: A single accepted counter directly selects the repetition count.

reachability.summary: Reachable from attacker-controlled DOCX through ordinary public rendering and the agent-view formatter, without raised limits or high list levels.
reachability.entrypoint: Rendering and DOCX agent-view list formatting
reachability.outcome: Very large marker allocation and worker failure.

attackPath.summary: Supply a normal-level numbering definition with Chicago format, a very large start and a %1 label token, then render or read the document through the shared formatter.

remediationTests: Refuse oversized Chicago starts and overrides at level zero before allocating a large label.
Exercise the same malformed counter through rendering and agent-view reading, and retain ordinary Chicago cycles.

originalCandidate.originalEvidence: src/convert/mod.rs:6015-6018 chicago_label(n) returns MARKS[i % 4].repeat(i / 4 + 1) for unrestricted u32 n. A numbering level with numFmt='chicago', start='4294967295', lvlText='%1' makes ~3 GiB string (1,073,741,824 repetitions of 3-byte ‡) from a few XML digits. Unlike high ilvl, works at normal ilvl=0, so capping levels alone does not fix it. Tracing parse_num_level/format_num.
